title: What If You Were Born as King Leonidas? | The 300 Spartans

paras: If you were born as Leonidas, you'd be raised to kill from the age of seven.
Become a king you were never supposed to be.
And with three hundred men, stand in front of the biggest army the world had ever seen.
But right now?
You're a baby in Sparta.
No shield. No spear. Not even a chance of the crown.
You're born around 540 BC, the son of King Anaxandridas.
But you're his third son.
Your big half-brother Cleomenes will be king. Then your brother Dorieus.
Nobody expects anything from you.
Remember that.
And in Sparta, even being born is a test.
Elders look at every newborn baby.
If they think it's weak, the story goes, it's left on a mountainside to die.
They look at you.
And they let you live.
You're seven.
And you're taken from your home.
Every Spartan boy goes to the agoge, the training.
Except the heir to the throne.
He's allowed to skip it.
You're not the heir. So you go.
Your head is shaved.
You get one thin cloak a year.
No shoes. Even in winter.
You sleep on reeds you rip out of the river with your bare hands.
And they feed you barely enough to survive.
On purpose.
They want you to steal food.
If you're caught, you're whipped.
Not for stealing.
For getting caught.
You learn to talk in as few words as possible.
To this day, short, sharp answers are called laconic, after your homeland.
Remember that too.
At twenty, you're a full Spartan soldier.
You eat in a mess hall with fifteen men, every night, for the rest of your life.
Black soup made with pork and blood.
People who taste it understand why Spartans aren't afraid to die.
Your father dies.
Your half-brother Cleomenes becomes king.
Your brother Dorieus is so angry he isn't chosen, he sails away to start his own city.
He's killed in Sicily.
One day, messengers come from the king of Persia, the biggest empire on earth.
They ask Sparta for earth and water.
A sign that you surrender.
Sparta throws them down a well.
There's your earth and water. Dig it out yourselves.
You marry Cleomenes' daughter, Gorgo.
She's young, and she's sharper than almost anyone in Sparta.
When she was just a little girl, she warned her father not to take a foreign bribe.
He listened.
Once, a woman from another city asks her why Spartan women are the only women who rule their men.
Gorgo answers: because we're the only ones who give birth to men.
Then Cleomenes goes mad.
His family locks him in wooden stocks.
He talks a guard into giving him a knife.
And he cuts himself to death.
The heir is dead.
The brother is dead.
The boy nobody expected anything from?
He's king.
Around 490 BC, you become king of Sparta.
You're about fifty.
Quick pause.
You asked for Leonidas, and here he is.
Who should live next? Drop a name in the comments.
And if you want a new life every few days, subscribe.
Ten years later, Persia comes back.
Their new king, Xerxes, is bringing one of the largest armies the ancient world has ever seen.
So big, people say it drinks rivers dry.
But it's the time of a sacred festival in Sparta.
The army isn't allowed to march.
So you go anyway.
With three hundred men.
You pick only fathers who have living sons.
So no family line ends.
Before you leave, Gorgo asks what she should do if you don't come back.
You tell her: marry a good man, and have good children.
You march north with your three hundred, picking up allies along the way.
Around seven thousand Greeks in total.
Against maybe a hundred thousand Persians, or more.
You stop at a place called Thermopylae.
The Hot Gates.
A narrow pass between the mountains and the sea.
Here, it doesn't matter how big an army is.
Only a few men can fight at once.
Xerxes waits four days, sure that you'll run.
Then he sends a message.
Hand over your weapons.
You answer with two words.
Come and take them.
One of your soldiers is told the Persian arrows will be so many, they'll block out the sun.
Good, he says.
Then we'll fight in the shade.
On the fifth day, the Persians attack.
Wave after wave, into a wall of bronze shields and long spears.
Your men fake a retreat, turn around, and cut down whoever chases them.
The ones nobody expected anything from, remember?
That's what you trained for.
Xerxes sends his best soldiers, ten thousand elite fighters called the Immortals.
They fail too.
People say Xerxes jumps up from his throne three times, terrified for his army.
Two days.
And the pass still holds.
Then a local Greek named Ephialtes goes to Xerxes, hoping for a reward.
He tells him about a goat path through the mountains.
A way around you.
That night, the Immortals walk it.
By morning, you're about to be surrounded.
You send most of the Greeks home.
But you stay.
Your three hundred stay.
So do around seven hundred men from a small city called Thespiae, and a few hundred from Thebes.
The story goes that you tell your men to eat a good breakfast.
Because tonight, they'll dine in the underworld.
On the third day, you don't wait in the pass.
You march out into the open, straight at the Persians.
Spears break.
You fight with swords.
Then with your hands and teeth.
You're about sixty years old.
And you fall.
Your men fight over your body four times to drag it back.
Then they pull back to a little hill.
And fight until there's no one left.
Xerxes is furious.
He has your head cut off and your body put on display.
He wins the battle.
But it cost him days, and thousands of men, and his army's nerve.
The next year, the Greeks crush the Persian fleet at Salamis.
Then a Spartan-led army beats them on land.
Persia never invades Greece again.
At Thermopylae, the Greeks put up a stone with two lines on it.
Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by.
That here, obedient to their laws, we lie.
You were the third son.
The one who was never meant to be king.
So you went through the training heirs were allowed to skip.
And that's exactly why, when the biggest army in the world came, you didn't run.
You lost the battle, your life, and even your head.
And twenty-five centuries later, we still know your name.
So tell me.
Was staying at Thermopylae bravery, or a king who'd already decided to die?
